t: #2193 Minimum Number of Moves to Make Palindrome — Editorial
o:
We may only swap adjacent characters, and we want the minimum number of swaps to turn `s` into a palindrome. A classic fact: the minimum number of adjacent swaps to rearrange a string into a target arrangement equals the number of inversions relative to that target, so we should choose the *best* palindrome target and count inversions efficiently.

Example 1 (`"aabb"`): matching the two `a`s costs 1 swap and the two `b`s cost 1 swap, total 2. Example 2 (`"letelt"`): moving the last `t` next to the first `t` costs 1 swap, then the `l`s cost 1 swap — total 2.

With `n ≤ 2000`, an O(n²) greedy simulation is fast enough, so we avoid the heavier Fenwick-tree inversion counting.
k: Greedy: fix the outermost pair first — take the leftmost character and bring its last occurrence to the right end.
If a character occurs an odd number of times, its leftover copy belongs in the center and can be dropped for free.
Adjacent-swap distance between two arrangements = number of inversions, so local cheapest pairing is globally optimal.

a.i: Repeatedly look at the first character `c`. Find its last occurrence at index `j`; moving it to the last position costs exactly `len-1-j` swaps (everything between shifts left by one, cancelling pairwise). Delete both matched characters and repeat. A character whose only remaining occurrence is itself is dropped — it will sit in the middle of the palindrome.
s: Convert the string to a mutable list.
While non-empty, find the last index `j` of the first character.
If `j == 0`, delete the head (center character) and continue.
Otherwise add `len-1-j` to the answer, delete positions `j` and `0`.
a.t: O(n²) — each iteration scans for the last occurrence and deletes from a list; n ≤ 2000 makes this fine.

w: Use the greedy simulation in an interview — it is simple and provably optimal because adjacent-swap distance equals inversion count against the chosen pairing. Pitfalls: forgetting the odd-count center character (just drop it, it costs nothing extra), and using `find_first` instead of the *last* occurrence. Follow-up: for n up to 1e5, count inversions with a Binary Indexed Tree over the chosen target permutation for O(n log n).
